The Pleated sea squirt Styela plicata is a sessile tunicate common in fouling communities along temperate and subtropical coasts, and its life-history traits have been documented in several laboratory studies. At a water temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C], newly released tadpole larvae undergo metamorphosis and settle after approximately 0.6 days [ab = approximately 0.6 days], a remarkably brief free-swimming phase that reflects the species’ reliance on rapid substrate colonization. The resulting oozoids have a wet weight at birth of just 0.0000245 grams [Wwb = 0.0000245 grams], an extremely small initial mass that is consistent with the minute egg diameter of about 0.15 millimeters from which they develop. This negligible birth mass underscores the substantial physiological challenge of transitioning from a yolk-dependent embryo to a filter-feeding juvenile, and it imposes a steep early growth trajectory. Field observations indicate that individuals often settle on artificial substrates such as pier pilings and aquaculture nets, where competition for space with other sessile organisms is intense.

As the juvenile grows, it undergoes a period of rapid somatic expansion before reaching the size at which gametogenesis can begin. Reproductive maturity in Styela plicata is attained at a body length of approximately 4 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4 centimeters], a threshold that marks the onset of gonadal development and the capacity to produce viable gametes. This length at puberty is relatively modest compared to the maximum body size the species can achieve, and it suggests that individuals allocate resources toward reproduction relatively early in their growth trajectory. The time from settlement to reaching this pubertal length is influenced strongly by temperature; under warmer summer conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 61 days [tp = approximately 61 days], a rapid maturation that facilitates multiple generations within a single warm season. In contrast, during cooler winter months, the same developmental process may extend to around five months, highlighting the pronounced thermal sensitivity of this species’ ontogeny.

Adult individuals of Styela plicata can ultimately attain a total body length of up to 8 centimeters [Li = up to 8 centimeters], making it one of the larger solitary ascidians in its fouling community guild. The corresponding ultimate wet weight reaches approximately 60 grams [Wwi = approximately 60 grams], representing a massive increase from the initial birth mass of just a few hundred-thousandths of a gram. This dramatic size range illustrates the extraordinary growth potential of the species when food resources are abundant and environmental conditions are favorable. The maximum body length is typically observed in older, reproductively active adults that have had several months of continuous feeding. It is noteworthy that individuals in crowded, space-limited environments rarely attain these upper size limits, as intraspecific competition for both food and attachment area can constrain growth. Nevertheless, under optimal laboratory conditions or in relatively unoccupied natural substrates, these asymptotic dimensions are regularly recorded.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified under controlled conditions at 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C], allowing estimation of its maximum reproductive rate. Field and laboratory data suggest that a single adult, releasing approximately 6850 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 6850 eggs per day] under optimal food availability, can achieve this high daily fecundity. The daily output is sustained throughout the breeding season, reflecting a continuous spawning pattern rather than a series of discrete clutches. Such a substantial investment in offspring production is energetically demanding and likely contributes to the relatively short post-reproductive period observed in this species.

The overall lifespan of Styela plicata has been determined in long-term laboratory rearing studies at a stable 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. Under these conditions, individuals reach a maximum longevity of 183 days [am = 183 days], a relatively short duration that is typical of many small, fast-growing solitary ascidians at a temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. Most mortality occurs after the reproductive peak, with adults typically surviving only an additional three to four months following the attainment of sexual maturity. This life-history pattern—rapid growth, early reproduction, and a compressed lifespan—is characteristic of an opportunistic, colonizing species that thrives in ephemeral or disturbed habitats. The 183-day lifespan (183 days) [am = 183 days] places Styela plicata among the shorter-lived members of its family, and it emphasizes the selective advantage of diverting energy toward early and prolific reproduction rather than extended somatic maintenance at a temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C]. This strategy proves highly successful in the dynamic fouling communities where the species is most abundant.
